utterances.text: Because the police and army were in these positions at Kodra e Geshtenjeve and could have fired from any of these positions if we tried to enter the village itself. And even the next day, in the morning, it was difficult for us to move because of these positions which could have fired on this road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Since your forces returned to Racak as early as 1600 hours, that takes care of that reason. And then this other reason, you mentioned snow. What snow are you talking about when yesterday on the videotape we saw that the grass was there and that the grass was yellow and there was only traces of snow? So could it possibly be that these traces of snow were a hindrance for your movements? There was no snow? The footage that we saw yesterday. And when the camera showed the environment, one could see the yellow colour everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer, instead of these long questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was January, although it looks as if it was summer, and it was very cold. It was winter. There was snow, especially in those mountains. There was not much snow seen in the pictures because of the trampling of the area, and the media had been there the next day, but during the night it had been very cold and there was snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's not dwell on that much longer. It's quite obvious. The answer is quite obvious and clear. You say that then William Walker came to verify the massacre. When you say that he came to verify the massacre, that is to say that you first established that there was a massacre and then Walker came to verify it. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not verify that. However, what happened in Recak, based on information coming from the civilians, was able to be verified the very next day, in the morning, when the OSCE team travelled to the site, followed by members of the media. And William Walker, besides all of this, had received information from his own teams, and that's why he appeared in person: to try and verify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it perhaps the truth that you brought some bodies there of persons who were killed as they moved about and as they were engaged in fighting, and then you brought Walker in to verify that they were there? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we had not been there at the crime scene. The first to arrive there were the OSCE team, and with them was Fehmi Mujota. As can be seen from the footage shown here yesterday, all the massacred can be seen, the blood can be seen, the wounds from the bullets can be seen, and all the stains left on their clothes can be seen. Everything can be seen over there. And it would have been impossible to do that, additionally because of the fact that they were inhabitants of Recak, and in our units we had members of the KLA from Recak, and it would have been impossible for them to try and imagine what you're imagining there, to try and stage up this kind of massacre. Don't try and impose this on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you come to put your case in important matters such as this, be unequivocal, not: "Is it perhaps the truth?" You should put it to the witness. This is your case that they brought bodies that were killed to that particular point. So I suggest to you, don't be equivocal about it, because that is your case. Put it clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did say it clearly, loud and clear and unequivocally: Did they bring the bodies in and then call him to verify it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the version that I see, you had: "Is it perhaps the truth?" When you're putting your case, you must put it unequivocally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I've presented it unequivocally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The members of KLA who are inhabitants of Racak, although not all of them were inhabitants of Racak, all the persons killed. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were soldiers from Recak, but the ones who were killed in Recak were civilians from Recak, with the exception of nine soldiers. One can see that there were people from Mullopolc, from Kacanik. So there were soldiers from everywhere, as well as there were soldiers from Recak in other units. Those people who were killed there were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I claim that they were members of the KLA and you claim that they were civilians. I think that that has been explained sufficiently clearly. At 12.00, you went to meet Walker in Petrovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the first time you met Walker since this operation had started in Racak?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first time I had met Mr. Walker. I met him at the crime scene, where I went, and the meeting itself took place at 12.00, in Petrova. It was the first time that I was meeting Mr. William Walker.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the question please be repeated. The interpreters couldn't hear it because it came at the same time when the witness was answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you meet at the place where you claim was the crime scene? Was it before the meeting or after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before the meeting, at about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was when Walker came there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is where I saw him, and that is where he requested a meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday you claimed, and today you repeated it, that when Walker came there, the only member of the KLA who was there was Fehmi Mujota. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. However, during those few moments, I arrived there, as well as my two bodyguards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, that means that you came there and you met him there. So it wasn't only Fehmi Mujota. You were there, and some other members of the KLA, when Walker was touring the place and when - we can see it on the video footage - as he is examining the persons who were killed, the bodies.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That footage also shows my arrival there subsequent to the arrival of Walker. The interval could have been brief after the arrival of Walker. It is true that I went there and met Walker at the place where the incident took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you come to the place where this incident occurred? How much time later? After Walker, that is.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, because I don't know what time Walker reached the place. So I can only suppose that the interval must have been brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had he already come to the place where the incident had occurred or did you tour the place where the incident had occurred together with him?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw him there. He went on his own and verified them, and only after that I met him in Recak for a minute or two, where he requested a meeting, and I said, "Let's go somewhere and sit down and talk."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that means that Walker first toured the place where the incident had occurred, and it was only after he had finished touring it that you saw him there at the place where the incident had occurred; right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had checked all the bodies before meeting me. All I know is that I met him there at the place where this incident occurred. Our eyes met. We did not talk. We only had a minute or two near the mosque together, where I said, "This conversation should not take place standing," because even at that stage I was under huge emotional stress, and I demanded that the meeting be held in Petrova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, let's clarify one thing, and let's hurry up, because we haven't got much time left. Walker toured the place where the incident occurred before you had come. Did he tour it once again after you came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are wasting time on this particular point. We've spent many minutes on it. It's a small point. What the witness has said is that he arrived there subsequently to Mr. Walker. He doesn't know what Mr. Walker did first. He may have toured the scene, he may not. It seems to me you're not going to get any further on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that at the time when Walker was touring the place where the incident had occurred, there were no members of the KLA who were present, apart from Fehmi Mujota? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not in uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never wore a uniform, because he was a political personality of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So when Walker was touring the place where the incident had occurred, there were no uniformed members of the KLA with him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was me and two other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not tour the place with Walker, did you? You said that he had toured it without you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did not go shoulder to shoulder with Walker. He was conducting his own business. What I went there to do was to verify the information that had been reaching the zonal command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. I haven't got time now, but I'm going to give you a cassette, when a few members of the KLA who are in uniform can be seen as Walker is touring the scene. But I'm not going to do that now because I haven't got enough time. So let's proceed. The meeting with Walker was attended by Fehmi Mujota and who else?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also the translator for Mr. Walker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct that you shot at Serbs from two mortars as they were boarding the bodies into a truck by the mosque in order to have the investigation, the post-mortem carried out and the forensic examination?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did fire, and we did stage an assault, because this was a crime committed over the citizens of Recak. And the attack, in order to retrieve the bodies, came before agreement had been reached on what kind of experts ought to come -- let me clarify at some length, please, because this is significant. They started their attack even before negotiations had been completed, had been insisting that the forensics -- the forensic team that ought to come -- to go and verify ought to include Serbians as well as The Hague Tribunal. You very well know that Louise Arbour, the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, that is not what I've been asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask you to tell the witness to answer my questions only. I haven't got time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that 17 people were killed during the attack, that you killed 17 Serbs then.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know how many Serbs were killed, but the fighting, which we call the fighting over the bodies, was conducted by our own units, of which I was a part, and we assaulted the vehicles of the Serbian police and army. We used various kinds of weapons, including two mortars. And we went into this kind of a wedge-like assault inside the Serbian positions. We were not aware of the number of people killed, but from the information coming from OSCE verifiers the very next day, we gathered that there were about 17 soldiers -- Serbian soldiers or police that had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You wrote here that -- that 17 of them were killed and that 11 of you were shooting from a distance not greater than 300 metres at the investigating Judge and these people that were boarding the bodies -- that were loading the bodies into the truck. That's on page 17 but, I'm not going to dwell on that longer. I'm going to skip some questions because -- you say that Danica Marinkovic tried to land in a helicopter but she didn't manage to because you started firing at her. And I imagine that that is not being challenged now; right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first clarify that in the statement, I say that verifiers, without specifying who they were, told of 17 people killed while further below I say that our own observers only related that they were hearing Serbian voices coming from Serbian police and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on to the next point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Is it correct that on the 18th of January, our forces broke down your positions from Petrovo and Krajkovo and Rance and that part of your forces went to Rance and Mulliri e Kurtishit, as it says here; is that right? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... stand this. Once more, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please give me a brief answer. Is it correct that on the 18th of January, our forces broke down the positions of your forces from Petrovo all the way to Rance and that you went to your back-up positions? Is that right or is that not right? It's on page 16, in the last paragraph. "On the 18th of January, they managed to break our positions from Petrovo all the way to Krajkovo and Rance. A part of our KLA soldiers went to their back-up positions in Rance," et cetera, et cetera. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is true that we withdrew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then you claim -- you say: "The Serbs entered Rance on that day, the 18th, and the KLA --" that is to say you -- "killed 20 Serbs." That is what it says here as well at the end of this paragraph that I've been quoting to you. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you wish, I can clarify how that occurred. I could tell you which positions we were occupying, because the territory between Rance, Petrova, and Recak is a mountainous area and the withdrawal of Serbian soldiers took place via the Mulliri e Kurtishit, as it is called, and towards Lluzhak. And all those were the positions that we occupied on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that the Serbs agreed to hand over all the bodies after the post-mortem would be carried out and that the foreign forensic experts joined in, and I imagine that that is not being contested in any way. And that on that day, in February 1999, a large number of civilians attended the funeral, that Walker was there, and that you were there in uniform with three uniformed soldiers escorting you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, let me say that it was insisted that the bodies be released one by one so that -- but the families of those massacred did not agree to this. They wanted the -- the whole number to be returned as a group, as they were taken. Some days later, they were released as a group, and their burial occurred in February. William Walker attended this funeral, and I also attended it, albeit briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I didn't ask you that. You've given a sufficient answer. Why did you arrest a number of civilians, then, at the funeral? Just briefly, please. Albanians.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not arrest any civilians. We detained for a very brief period. We took the risk of intervention of Serbian paramilitaries of the kind of the Black Hand in the midst of the civilians in order to cause incident that could have huge repercussions and result in another massacre. So what we did is we detained for a few hours, until the funeral was over, all the people -- all the suspects that took part in that funeral. All of them were released within the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. These stories about the Black Hand and paramilitary formations are stories we've already heard. They are quite picturesque and equally inaccurate, untrue. But since you've mentioned it, you claim that all politicians, and you are referring to Serb politicians, had military units in Kosovo. I'm going to quote page 9 to you, this big paragraph in the middle. You say: "Kostunica posed for a photograph when he toured the Serb troops in Kosovo during the conflict. He wore a bandolier on his chest, wearing an ammunition belt across his chest, holding an automatic weapon. I saw Seselj on television in a military uniform several times visiting his own units." Are you referring to Kosovo yet again?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Kostunica did pose, and that appeared in the dailies bearing those images. If you want, Your Honour, we can procure a copy. We can also find the recordings of Serbian radio television showing Seselj in military uniform inspecting his own units, as was the case with Raznjatovic, nicknamed Arkan, a member of the Serbian parliament, who also was shown by the public media. I can also say here that I have volunteered to the Court some other information which shows the fund of so-called Dragan where workers of the Kokollari family funded or contributed to this fund. And according to the information that I have, it was part of a paramilitary formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, and that's my point, all politicians have military units. That's what you said. Are you aware of the fact that no politicians had any military units and that you've invented all of this, all of this about the paramilitary units? Why did you invent all of this, the Black Hand and things like that? What do you need that for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I can't find this particular comment in the statement. No doubt I can be referred to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's page 9 that he's looking at. Your Honour's probably found that. It's in the middle of the page, and it may be that there's a different interpretation to be put on it than that which the accused advances, and I'll probably deal with it in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end of the paragraph, it says: "All the politicians have military units. They all attacked Kosovo in some way." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I have found it. It's at the bottom -- just -- don't interrupt. It's at the bottom of the English page 9. What -- Mr. Buja, what it says: "The paramilitaries walked in uniform unchallenged by police and army in all the towns and villages. All the politicians have military units. They all attacked Kosovo in some way." That's the English translation. Can you clarify what you meant by that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant there was the Serbian political hierarchy. And I described some of the politicians like Raznjatovic, Arkan, a member of the Serbian parliament, as was Vojislav Seselj. And also at that time when Kostunica posed with a weapon in his hands, he was a member of the Serbian parliament. And I'm referring to senior members of the hierarchy. And as far as we know, in former communist -- in former communist states, all senior politicians also bore a military rank as reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you mean that citizens of Yugoslavia have some kind of a military rank as reservists? Is this some special bit of information?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not understand what the point was of this assertion the citizens of Yugoslavia, as reservists who had served their military service, who had done their military service, have some rank in the army. What's the point?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was additional information, because the so-called paramilitary units that belonged to Arkan and Seselj were also shown in your radio and television station, and the visits of those politicians to these units were also shown. And also, these units were never in any way hampered by the Serbian police and the army. And it can easily be inferred that all those paramilitary units received the commands from yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have one minute left, which is time for one question more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you say? One more question only? Please. Mr. May, I think that the very fact that you bring such a witness here shows that this institution of yours supports the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber brings no witnesses. The Prosecution are responsible for that. Now, have the amici any questions? Bearing in mind that there is the pressure of time. Mr. Tapuskovic, if you have any questions -- if you have any questions, please deal with them as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please state that I have objected, and you will not let me speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I don't know if I can complete very quickly. I'll try to do it within a few minutes, but I do need some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, would you please try and complete at least so there's time for re-examination before the adjournment, which is at quarter past. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Buja, I would like to start by asking you to look at the map once again. And so far, we haven't shown the following: Can you tell us where your base was? Can you show us that place, and can you show us the place where the bodies of 24 people were found? If you can show us this on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how many metres are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The base was here. There was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests the witness to draw near the microphone. The interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you speak into the microphone, please. Could you point out for us, if you would, if you can, the base and then the ravine in which the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was the base here where the soldiers were killed. And here is where the civilians were killed. There were civilians killed there and there, and here too. There were civilians killed in various parts of Recak, but most were in that place that is indicated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tapuskovic. You pointed 2, number 2, as your base; is that right? Number 2 was commented as crime scene 2. Is it right or could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can explain, because there were eight people -- eight soldiers killed here and also six civilians, including Hanemshah Mujota that I described. One was Mehmet Mustafa, the owner of the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't need to go into those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following: What is the distance in metres? You showed us, and it seems to be very close to your base. How many metres away is it from the base to the place where 23 bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's between 500 and 1.000 metres, because it's a very high hill that has to be crossed between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted you to point to that on the map. And now, please, Mr. Buja, here you described in detail a very important matter. Just a minute, please. On page 4 of your statement, the English version. The English [as interpreted] version is page 4 as well. You described and you gave the number of seven zones of responsibility, and you also listed their names. So there were seven zones.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were seven zones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the number of people who at different times belonged to zone 6, which was under your command, was between 1.400 and 1.700 people. That's what you said today as well. But you also said the following: "All other zones had more people." My question is this: If all other zones had had more people and there was a total of seven zones and let's say that each zone had 2.000 people, is it true, then, that the KLA had a total of approximately 14.000 people at that time?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can't say that, that there were 40.000 people, because it's -- I heard 40.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. I said 14.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it might be about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that at the same time when the incident in Racak took place that you had approximately that number of people?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of soldiers in all the zones at that time because I was merely responsible for my own zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. However, I would like to know something else as well. You said here --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Your Honours, this can be found on page 7, paragraph 3, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say here as follows: "Then an order came in from the Main Staff of the KLA for mobilisation of Kosovo, because this order was given at the beginning of the NATO intervention that everyone 18 years and older had to be mobilised." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this order was public, but it was impossible to mobilise the entire population because of the lack of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to hear your answer regarding the following: Were there members of the KLA that wore civilian clothes? Was there a large number of those?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not a large number. But there was the case of Fehmi Mujota, or one or two others, whose task was to work with civilians, and it was difficult to work with civilians in uniform because of the danger of attacks. But except in these special cases, all members of the KLA had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on page 3, paragraph 2 from the top, the English version, you say that you had no trouble recruiting people, men or women, recruiting them for the KLA, but that on occasion, you were forced to take in soldiers without military training, and they were generally assigned only to dig trenches and build bunkers.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true, because we didn't have any problem recruiting soldiers, because there was a great flood of young people to become members of the KLA. But we lacked weapons. And when our unarmed units made bunkers, we did this at the time of the NATO intervention, because we had to expand because of the great influx of civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they didn't even have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them did have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the number of those who did not have uniforms? Because you also told us that at the end of the war, you had an entire brigade that was not uniformed.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can give the number, because we called a brigade a very small number of soldiers. Our largest brigade was 1.200 soldiers, whereas there were some -- normal brigades were 400 to 500 men. And at the end of the war there was a brigade in the Nerodime operational zone, including the people mobilised in Jezerc and Mullopolc, and there was another brigade in the Kacanik area. And if you were to gather all these people together, you might have formed one brigade out of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you something regarding Racak. I know that it was a day in January. It was cold. Two residents of Racak, witnesses here, told us yesterday that when the shooting started, they went out in the clothes that they had on them at that time, and 24 people that were killed in Racak on that day, based on what we have here as not contentious, wore double socks and three layers of clothing. So how do you explain that? Is it something typical for people who go to the mountains or for people who are in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is normal in this area, because winter is very cold, and people normally dress up warm because of the bitter cold. They were taken from their homes, and so they put on their thickest clothes, because they thought that they would be arrested. And that's what happened in the case of the Recak civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said yesterday that what took place in Racak was a planned operation of ethnic cleansing; however, you don't mention anything of this kind in your statement. You mention other things that we heard here. You said that this is something that was a result of the policemen that were killed, and you never said before that this was a planned operation of ethnic cleansing. Why didn't you ever mention this before?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I emphasised the things that the investigator asked me about, and I didn't enlarge on explanations of this kind; I replied to questions. And I would welcome other questions to explain what the operation was really like, such as the operation on the plain, where there was no KLA at all. This was an operation of ethnic cleansing, as were the massacres in Hallac and Sllovi and other places. These were all part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we saw the weapons on the ELMO. It was manufactured by whom? Can you tell us? The weapons that we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can't say what kind of production they were because you can't really see on the television, but they rather resembled automatic rifles known as Kalashnikovs. But you can't really check from the television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the quantity of weapons does not correspond with the number of nine KLA soldiers that were killed, but does it correspond with the number of 47 people that you had in your base?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course it doesn't correspond. But let me say clearly that our soldiers had weapons, and four automatic rifles were taken from our soldiers. And I said that a 12.7 and a 7.9 were taken, and not the ones that we saw. Because I stressed yesterday that our soldiers didn't have rifles with bayonets, and it would have been extremely unusual to find any weapon with a bayonet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Buja, just now, when asked by Mr. Milosevic, you spoke about the 27 Serb policemen that were killed in Rance, and then you spoke about 17 that were killed in front of the mosque. However, in your statement, you also said that seven Serbs were killed in Pustenik, seven Serbs. That's what you said in your statement, page 17.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is about Serbian soldiers and police killed in fighting at Pustenik. This position was in Kacanik municipality, not far from Han i Elezit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So together with the two policemen that were killed on the 15th, the day of the event in Racak, we come to a figure of 47 policemen that were killed during those days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure that all these people were killed, because the number 17 said to have been killed at Recak, we were unable to confirm this figure. It was the OSCE team that issued this figure. Nor can we confirm the number of 25 soldiers in Rance, because there was firing all the time, and from the position where we were fighting, it's very hard to tell if anybody was killed or not. But we didn't have soldiers killed in our area that we were able to certify as killed, and people died in their own positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one more question, Mr. Buja. What was your view of the events that took place in the very beginning of the NATO bombing? What was your opinion, since you were a soldier? What impact did it have on the movements of the population or on the behaviour, attitude of people?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were pleased at the start of the NATO bombing because they saw some hope. They could see that they had a prospect of freedom, not to be mistreated, killed, massacred. And so the NATO intervention represented a hope that life in Kosova could become better in the future, and we soldiers felt the same. Because our intention was not to wage war. War was imposed on us. So we wanted this war to finish as soon as possible, and it was in this light that we saw the NATO intervention, the Rambouillet meeting, and the hope for political agreements. Our hope was to be free and to have this fighting behind us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both Albanians and Serbs got killed by NATO bombs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true, and it is regrettable that people of both peoples were killed. So let this be a lesson for both sides to live in one state in freedom and democracy. And I think that the Serbian people will understand that it was -- that bringing the international community and the KLA was an impulse towards bringing the international community and therefore played a constructive role [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you deal with it before the adjournment, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll do my very best. I don't actually have a great deal to ask, just a few matters. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been asked questions about ethnic cleansing, you've identified other locations where you say ethnic cleansing occurred. Just in a sentence or so, what, if any, similarities were there between events in those other locations and what happened at Racak?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The connection is that civilians -- the same kind of civilians were killed in these places, but these other places had similar cases but have not been mentioned yet in this Court. There was Ribar i Madh, where civilians were killed, where a very similar operation of Recak was conducted, because it was part of a Horseshoe operation, involving attacks on Banulla, Ribar, Recak, and other villages in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked just now, or a little bit before just now, about 47 people in Racak for the KLA, of whom we know nine were killed. The remainder, when deployed, would they leave their weapons behind in Racak or would they take their weapons, their arms, with them?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When KLA members based in Racak were deployed to various locations, did they take their arms with them or did they leave them behind at the base?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, KLA soldiers, if they had a short rest, took their weapons with them, whereas when they went home for a longer period, they left their weapons behind at the command post. This was our normal military practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were being asked that question, I think, in connection with the arms cache shown on the video we looked at yesterday. Is there any possibility of any of those arms that we saw yesterday being arms of the KLA that, for example, had been left behind in the base?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the KLA soldiers were there, and the number of weapons was far, far too big. And I explained yesterday that we didn't have any kind of arsenal of this kind in the Rance and Recak units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Kwon's question about site 2. You told us about how the bodies of soldiers were recovered, the bodies of civilians were not recovered. Were they in the same general location at site 2?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were at the same position at our base, but the soldiers only had the right to take soldiers' bodies, and there were civilian organisations that dealt with civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you can judge it, were the civilians killed at the same time as the soldiers at site 2 or at a different time?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians were killed at the same time, in the same period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we reached the issue of the map, could you look at the map on the left-hand side? Could you go to the map, and with the movable microphone. You notice number 6 on the left-hand side? That is the ravine. Many civilians were killed at that point. You recognise it? And number 7 is the location of your bunker. Is it right? Number 7 below. So your base is somewhere in the middle between the two points; is it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in order to go to the base, what way do the soldiers usually take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had a path and trenches connecting the base and the bunker. You can see this in the photographs that I can show, and that's how they got to the bunker. There were trenches here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From Petrovo, in order to go to the base from Petrovo, what way do you usually take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very difficult to follow the normal road because of the positions by the pine trees, but we used to approach from the rear, from Lluzhak. We went through Lluzhak to get in around here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you must go past the location of number 6 in order to get to the base? Number 6, the ravine place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because the Recak gorge is here, and here is the -- what we call the Krajkova road. And you can see -- you can go by the bunker to get to the base, and we always used this road, because it was a very dangerous journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please take your seat. I think I've only got three or four more questions, and I'll cut out some of them in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One thing: It's been suggested to you by the accused that either you did or that you could have attempted to re-enter the village, and you've rejected that proposition. Just remind us: The soldiers killed at location 2 were killed from the adjoining hills simply when they emerged onto the street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the soldiers, Serbian soldiers, positioned in this ring, the first soldiers were killed at the bunker with a Zolja, and from this position it was -- this was where all the soldiers were fired on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if you were in the street, for example, in the area of the base, were you vulnerable to being fired on by the Serb soldiers, in the way that the men were first thing in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were killed were killed here, because you can fire very easily from this position on the base, and that's where they were all killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The suggestion has effectively been made by the accused that all the people who died in Racak - and there are 45 listed in the indictment - at the various sites were KLA members. I'm not going to ask you to go through all of those names, but there are two women named: Lute Asllani and Hanumshah Mehmeti. Were those women members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 70-year-old Haki Metushi, was he a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then just to deal with one other name. There's been the suggestion that somebody called Mustafa has crept into the list of the civilians. The Mustafa of whom you spoke was the man aged, I think, 62, who insisted on becoming a member of the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mehmet Mustafa is his name, and the accused intentionally put in another Mehmet who is in the list of civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the name in the -- civilians. Yes. The name in the civilians is Mustafa. Well, the point's been made. Perhaps to follow on from His Honour Judge Kwon's question, because we don't have too much footage of the geography: How easy or difficult is the terrain between the base at figure 2 and the gully where the bodies were found? We can add to this by further footage or other evidence, but just tell us yourself: What's the terrain like up to the gully?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very steep and mountainous terrain, and it's very difficult to see this ravine from this position. It's a very jagged terrain, which you can see here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been asked questions about the killing of a police officer. We saw two reports yesterday, and there may be a third one being served when it's been translated, each of which come from the Serb side and refer to one policeman being seriously injured and no more casualties than that. Do you accept that there may have been in Racak one policeman seriously injured?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May have been injured from position number 10, but it's hard to imagine that there were Serbs killed in the morning fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I better make this the last question because of time. You've spoken of 1.400 KLA available generally. How many of those were in the area of Racak and available to fight in Racak?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ready to fight in Recak? This would have been a number of about 30, because there was also the catering staff who were unarmed. There were auxiliary and operational staff who were unarmed, and other soldiers who were in attendance there but who were also unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I have two questions. Before I move on, I'd like the registrar to exhibit this witness because it is cited so many times. Exhibit the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 212.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Racak were aware of the existence of KLA at their village?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have been able to know only that there were KLA soldiers in the upper part of the village near and above Recak, at this position here. But we didn't allow civilians to enter, so they wouldn't have been able to know the number of soldiers or the -- their positions because of the danger of them giving information under torture and mistreatment. So that's why we put our guard here, so that civilians wouldn't come in. So it would have been difficult for the residents of Recak to know the number of soldiers or to know where our positions were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You gave warnings and advised them to vacate before the attack to the villages. So they must have known after the attack there was some KLA base in their village.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They will have been able to know that there was something in Recak but not the number of soldiers. And when we warned them, we warned them, and they would have seen soldiers and the movement of soldiers, because this part where the soldiers moved over the hills to go to the Lluzhak gorge, they would have been visible to the residents of Recak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question is about Judge Marinkovic, the investigating Judge. Did your soldiers shoot at the police that accompanied the Judge?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know whether the Judge was there or not. We fired on the forces that fired on us and on the police and army that were positioned in Recak and around Recak and at the pine trees. So we fired at the police and soldiers that tried to enter this position here. And we were not aware of the presence of the Judge. But we saw trucks and Pinzgauers of the police and army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the Serb forces shoot first?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting going on throughout that day. On the 18th and 19th, there was constant fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, that concludes your evidence, and you're free to go. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well for the opportunity to give my evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We admit the statement under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your full name Isuf Zhuniqi?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Zhuniqi Isuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zhuniqi, did you make a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 4th of May of 1999, and did you, on the 31st of May of this year, go through that statement with a presiding officer of this Tribunal and acknowledge by your signature that it was true?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Can I, in those circumstances, produce the statement and the accompanying certification or attestation to become Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 213 and 213A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I, before reading the summary that I believe may have already been distributed, reorient the Chamber, as it has to divert from Racak for this witness to another location, by inviting you to look at page 10 of the atlas which has been placed on the overhead projector and in which I can explain as to its significance or potential significance for you. We can see Bela Crkva towards the right of the screen and immediately above a railway line, but otherwise roughly in the middle of the screen, slightly to the right, Bela Crkva, the railway line crossing over. I'll come back to the geography that's shown there in a second. Other villages that are referred to are, to the east and south Celine and Nogavac, and then to the west -- and I'm sorry, it's my mistake for not having checked the pronunciation of the town that is spelled X-e-r-x-e, but one can see that the other side of the railway line and to the west, and then south of that, sufficiently large to merit an orange marking, is the town Rogovo. If the Chamber now goes back to Bela Crkva, it will see -- it's not very clear to see, but it will see, apart from the roads marked in orange, that there is a blue line pretty well directly north-south that crosses or is crossed by the railway line, and it's at that crossing, as I understand it, the bridge there, that the awful events you're going to learn about unfolded. And can I next take you, for speed, to two photographs which can be laid on top of the map. They come from the second of the Bela Crkva binders, and they are within tab 1. And if the usher could place these on top of the map so as not to disturb the map because we may come back to it, in that order. First that one and then the second, and I'll explain them. The first photograph is a view of -- come down a little bit. The other way. Thank you. The view -- that's fine. Thank you. Is a view from Bela Crkva. And the winding tree line is, I think, the line of the river, the riverbed we're going to hear about. And one can see an almost straight line running left to right on the screen, and that is the railway line transected by the stream. So although what shows up on the map as a rather straight blue line as a stream, in fact it's a little bit wavy, as this tree line suggests. If we can put the second photograph on top and focus on the bridge itself, please. A little bit further up. Thank you. This shows the riverbed with the bridge and the railway line, and it was at that bridge that events unfolded. And I will read from the distributed summary, but I shan't necessarily read it word-for-word, in order to save a little time. The 42-year-old farmer witness comes from this village, the village of Bela Crkva. He spent some years in Switzerland, returning in 1996 in a position to purchase two buses and operate those buses as a private business, living in Bela Crkva with his wife, two daughters, two sons, his father and mother. Before the NATO bombing, the witness was unaware of conflicts in his village or the surrounding area, and there were indeed no Serb residents in Bela Crkva. At about 3.30 on the morning of the 25th of March, he woke to the sight and sound of 12 green VJ tanks coming from Orahovac, stopping by the mosque in his village. He gathered his family and other relations, immediate family and other relations, and led them to a hiding place in a field on the edge of the village where some 200 other villagers were also gathered. And from this position, they initially saw tanks leaving the village, leaving them to think that it might be safe to return, which they did. But 15 minutes later, the sound of automatic gunfire as close as 200 metres from them led the witness to gather his family again and take them to the stream that we have seen, if my understanding of the geography is correct. The stream was not so far from his house, but opposite to the direction he'd gone first for safety, for to have fled on this occasion to the woods would have taken his family in the direction of the gunfire. Some 700 villagers gathered in the stream. And the witness and his family walked for about a kilometre in the direction of Rogovo, which I have pointed out to the Chamber, occasionally taking cover because there appeared to be snipers firing in their general direction. Other gunfire and explosions could be heard. They reached the railway bridge and took shelter underneath it. At about 9.30, they observed, coming along in the same direction as that which they had come, a squad of some 16 policemen dressed in camouflage, wearing armbands. They were all armed with AK-47 assault rifles and had foot-long knives in scabbards attached to their belts. Some policemen also had pistols in their holsters, and one of them was recognised by the witness as a policeman ordinarily conducting normal duties in Orahovac. Shortly thereafter, the witness saw 13 Kosovo Albanian civilians who were not yet at the bridge but coming towards it, and the police in close proximity. They were fired on by the police, that 13, and only a 2-year-old boy survived. The people under the bridge were still locked into their position by sniper firing coming at their general direction. The police, who had thus committed the first 12 or so murders on this session, split into two groups and took firing positions on the banks on either side of the stream. An Albanian-speaking Serb policeman ordered them to go towards the police, and he then gave various orders: First that they should put their hands behind their heads and get out of the stream onto the railway line; then that they should be split into groups, women and children on one side and the men divided into two groups on the other. The men were ordered to strip to their underwear before being robbed of cash, jewellery, and identity documents. And one policeman, on finding Mr. Zhuniqi's passport, asked who was Isuf Zhuniqi, and the witness identified himself, to see his passport being torn up by the policeman, along with his identity card and driving licence, the policeman saying, "He might as well be dead." The Albanian-speaking policeman then ordered the Kosovar Albanian men to get dressed and to gather into a single group, instructed the women and children to leave, following the railway track, in the direction of Xerxe. When the women and children were about a hundred metres away but still in view, a man called Shendet Popaj was knocked to the ground and the leader of the police put his foot on Shendet Popaj's throat. That young man's uncle - he was, I think, under 20 - his uncle, who was a doctor from Bela Crkva, spoke to the leader of the police, saying, "Leave us alone. We are simple farmers. We are not KLA." Without a word, the police leader opened fire with a short burst from his assault rifle, hitting the doctor in the chest and killing him instantly, then turning his rifle on the young man lying on the ground under his boot. One shot to that young man's head killed him instantly. The remaining men, about 65 in total, were ordered to climb into the stream. The order to fire was then given, and so far as the witness could judge, all the policemen opened fire with automatic weapons. The witness was hit in the shoulder and fell down, with others falling on top of him, and he remained conscious but pretended to be dead during the shooting that continued immediately for some five minutes. When it stopped, policemen came into the stream and the witness heard some of them saying, and on different occasions, "Well, this one's breathing." That would be followed by a succession of single shots, and the witness remembers well over ten such shots. Later he heard one of the policemen say, "Well, now everyone is dead. Let's go." The witness waited for some 20 minutes, until everything was quiet. He got up and discovered the number of men around him who had been killed or who had sustained horrifying injuries from the gunfire. He witnessed over 50 bodies, of whom he is able to identify by name 41 in his statement. Despite his injuries, he was able to make his way to Xerxe, where he found his immediate family, where he was given first aid, although he suffered lapses into unconsciousness for the next few days. Police arrived. This led the witness to leave his family and go into hiding in the mountains, taking a basic medical kit with him, where he found 40 or so more villagers from Bela Crkva, also in hiding, and who informed him that the entire village can be destroyed, with only some two houses not burnt down. He felt able briefly to visit his family in Xerxe on the 31st of March, and there he walked to Nogavac, where there were many displaced persons who had been ordered by the Serbs to gather there. He was in a barn in that village when a low-flying plane bombed it, or bombed the area, causing the roof to collapse. From that he escaped, suffering some further shrapnel injuries to his arms and head. He then lost consciousness, waking days later in Kukes, in Albania, to which he had been taken by a relation who had found him unconscious. The witness then learned of the bullet that remained lodged in his shoulder. The witness's statement states that there had been no KLA presence in Bela Crkva, but he was never a member of the KLA himself, although a younger brother of his, with whom he had not spoken for some 12 months, had been a member some time prior to the campaign. The binder contains -- the Bela Crkva binder contains photographs of the x-rays and of the condition of the witness as injured, tabs, I think, 4, 5, and 6. That's the summary. There will now perhaps be further questions from the accused for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you said that before the 24th of May, although you were aware of the incidents that had occurred in Kosovo, in your village and in the surrounding area, nothing of significance was happening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No, nothing happened. I do not know what happened before -- I mean, nothing happened before the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your troubles started when the war started; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's look at the preceding period. How far away is Orahovac from your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Prizren is very far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about Prizren. Where did you get Prizren from? I asked about Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Prizren is 80 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand why you are giving me answers about Prizren. I'm asking about Orahovac. We looked at Bela Crkva on the map, and nearby, on the north-east, is Orahovac. So how far away is your village from Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Orahovac is very near. It's about ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your village is considered to be the outskirts of Orahovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: [In Serbian] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the period between the 17th and the 22nd of July, 1998, from the area of Orahovac, 39 Serbs and Albanians were kidnapped, abducted, by the KLA terrorists? You were driving there, so I assume that you are well aware of what was going on. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: On that particular day, the 16th, 1998, I was in Prizren, and I do not know what happened in my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not hear about these events, about the kidnappings of Serbs and Albanians in Orahovac in July 1998? You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I do not know anything. I was away until the OSCE arrived, and it's only after that that I returned to Bellacerkva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who Nuredin Kastrati is, a colleague of yours, a bus driver from the village of Naspale?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I do not know this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember an incident from April 1998 when a bus full of passengers was stopped by the KLA? April 1998. It's not important as to whether you know who the driver was. Do you remember the actual event?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: At that time the KLA did not stop the bus, but it was Serbian police and paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do know about that event, but your claim is that it was the Serbs that stopped the bus, right, in April 1998?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: At that time the KLA stayed in mountains. It did not descend upon the main roads, which were under the control of the Serbian police and paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Xhelaj Hajda is, nicknamed Toni?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about the KLA attack on Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No, I do not know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there is information that the KLA went through your village, inter alia, when they were about to attack Orahovac. Did they spend time there? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I do not know. I've never seen KLA members in the village of Bellacerkva, and I cannot say anything on this matter. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Skender Hoxha is?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I have never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the KLA was in that area of Orahovac? Did you ever hear his name?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard the name. I was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that when they were moving to attack Orahovac, the KLA not only spent some time in your village, but they also forcibly mobilised some villagers from your village? Have you heard of that? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I even said it earlier: On the 16th I was in Prizren, and I'm not aware of anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you don't know, never mind. You abide by your claim that nothing of significance happened in your village before the war broke out, so we have come to that conclusion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That is what the Serbian police and army did to the village of Bellacerkva, and I know that very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then. In your statement, you say that on the 25th -- you say in your statement that on the 25th of March, at 3.30 a.m., that is to say, in the middle of the night, you and your family members were awakened by the sound of tanks. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In order to refresh your memory, can you answer my question: Are you sure that it was the sound of tanks that awakened you, or was it the sound of the NATO bombing on the morning of the 25th, or rather, during the night, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, at 3.30 a.m., I woke up and I saw 12 military tanks, 12 Serbian military tanks, rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you left your house and went into the field that was on the outskirts of the village. Was that because you were afraid of tanks or was there some other reason for that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I was afraid of the tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The tanks just passed there. They didn't stay in the village. Is that right? Or at least, that's the way you had put it.

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I left the house and stayed away until the tanks left the village. It's only then that I returned back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We saw just now on that photograph that between the fields and the houses in Bela Crkva, there are trees. There's a forest. How can you see what was going on in the village when there was not a proper view from the field because of the trees in between?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No. When the village began to be burned, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about when you left as you were frightened of the tanks. And then you went back when you established that they had left. How could you see that when there is a forest between the fields and the village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I wasn't very far away, only about 200 metres away from the village, because it was pitch darkness. It hadn't dawned yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What time was it when you returned to the village again?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I returned at 5.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were away for a total of an hour and a half; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you leave your house again?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I left because about 200 metres away, I saw the village burning, and the police and paramilitaries were arriving on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of paramilitaries? I don't understand. What is that? Who are paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: You ought to know these things. I don't know what those paramilitaries were. The ones who slayed people, who killed people, those were the paramilitaries. The ones who shot people dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: In the -- in the village I was not fired upon, but I was fired upon at -- but people were fired upon at the ura, at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the bridge -- [French translation on English channel] -- is that right, the one that was displayed just a few minutes ago? [French translation on English channel]

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see -- [French translation on English channel]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are getting French on the English channel. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since there are people on the bridge and we can see how wide the railroad is, the bridge is not longer than ten metres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: It is longer than ten metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's say there's 11 metres. But it narrows further down, and there is a river underneath it; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could more than 700 inhabitants of the village hide underneath the bridge? Could you please explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: We were not under the bridge. There's an irrigation canal over there, and that is where we were hiding, not at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My understanding of your statement was that you were hiding underneath the bridge and that you stayed there for several hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it when you came to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: We arrived at the bridge at about 5.30 and stayed there until 9.15, until the Serbian police reached it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, something's not clear to me now. At 5.00 you came back to your house after the tanks had passed. That's what you wrote in your statement. And at 5.30, as early as that, you were under the bridge. So how is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: It is true that at 5.00 in the morning I was at home, and it took me half an hour to reach -- to reach the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say that at around 9.30 on that day, that morning, the policemen started toward you, the armed policemen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. And about 15 or 16 policemen were there, because I saw it with my own eyes. The Clirim family and Spahiu family of 12 members were killed at a distance of 150 metres and only a 2-year-old son survived the killing. Seven children died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you something else. When did the policemen start towards you? Was it at 9.30, as you claim in your statement? When did they start coming toward you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: At the time when the policemen came, they reached, yes, the railway that links Prizren and Xerxe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far were they from that bridge under which you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: The police were on the railway, and in Albanian, they told us to get up and approach. They said this to the first group. The second, larger group, consisting of elderly women and children was told the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far were the policemen?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: The policemen were about 20 or 30 metres away from us when we got up with our hands behind our backs to approach them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that they were armed with assault rifles. Can you tell me, please, what an assault rifle is?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: This is an automatic rifle that was used to shoot Albanian civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you specified that that was an AK-47.

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: This is what it was, because I saw it with my own eyes. It was an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But do you know that AK-47 is the very weapon used by the KLA terrorists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a separate point. The witness identified the rifles as AK-47s. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to remind you, Mr. May, that it was the previous witness, Mr. Buja, who is the chief of one of the terrorist groups, was the one who said that this was the weapon used by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't want to get into an argument about this. Are you suggesting that these were members of the KLA and not the police? Is that the point or some other point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm suggesting that this witness doesn't know what an assault rifle is, nor does he know what an AK-47 is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know what an AK-47 is? How were you able to recognise it, Mr. Zhuniqi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can describe it, because it was an automatic rifle, and I knew that only these kinds of weapons were used in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what colour is the butt of the rifle?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't see it at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just roughly. Is it dark or light?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've gone far enough on this. Find some other topic to ask the witness about. This is not important.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of a policeman who spoke Albanian, and you were sure that he was a Serb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I am sure that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what you claim that he was a Serb if he spoke Albanian?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't know his name at that time, but when I returned from Albania, I saw him, and his name was Nenad Matic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that under the bridge there was a shelter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that an air raid shelter?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No. There was an irrigation canal for agriculture, and people hid in this stream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means that this shelter was not prepared in advance. You qualified this irrigation canal as a shelter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: We used it as a shelter because it was an irrigation channel. We didn't think of preparing it for this purpose, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often did you use it as a shelter?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: This was the first and last time; on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never used it prior to that or after that, did you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: We didn't use it that way. I only used it to irrigate the fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did it come about then that all 700 of you went to that very spot to take shelter? Usually when there's a danger, people disperse in different directions. So how was it that all of you went to that very spot? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. Because we didn't have any other direction to go, because the Serbian army and police were on all sides, and the only way out was to go -- to go to the bridge of Belaje, either to go to the village of Xerxe or to Rogove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said here that the policemen who issued orders in Albanian ordered the police to fire at a group when a relative, I think it says here Clirim Zhuniqi, was killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Clirim Zhuniqi's family was there, as well his friend from Opterusha, Xhemal Spahiu, who was beaten and was killed. The only person of this group to survive was the 2-year-old Dardan Zhuniqi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But please answer me to my question. Why would a policeman issue orders in Albanian? Why would a Serb policeman issue orders in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
