utterances.text: It's not for the witness to say. He says the policeman did it. He cannot answer why the policeman did it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other Albanians in that group or other people who spoke Albanian other than that policeman issuing orders in Albanian? Did you hear somebody else speaking Albanian in that group?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I only heard him say, "Put your arms behind your back." And other times he spoke only in Serbian. It was only when he ordered us to put our hands behind our back that he spoke Albanian, when he shouted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I speak a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what language did he issue the order to fire? Was it in Albanian or in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you heard him order the firing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I heard him because I was only two metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they shot at you from a distance of two metres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I was two metres away from the point where he shot Nisim Popaj, the doctor, and Shendet Popaj, who was shot in the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far away was he when he issued an order to fire at you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: About two metres. When he gave the order for us all to enter the stream. And he gave, behind his back, the order to fire on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's not use that collective noun "civilian population." You said that there were 700 of you. So he ordered that fire should be opened at all 700 of you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No. He had divided the men from the women, and he told some old men to go to the village. And about a hundred metres from the village, he accomplished the execution of the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how many men did he execute then?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: By the stream, he -- they executed children, women, the elderly. Sixty people in all. Two of them were paralysed, and they were immobile. They couldn't move. And they were burned in their houses in Bellacerkva, in the house of Mehmet Zhuniqi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means that you claim that out of 700 people, after the men had been separated, he ordered that 60 of you should be executed. But not just men but women and children as well. Why were the men then separated before that, and how come that there were so few men in that group of 700?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Because the women and the children and the elderly were 150 metres from the point where Clirim Zhuniqi and his family were shot. And of this, there were 38 that were killed in my group, and there are only six survivors, and six were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So out of 700 people, 60 perished there as you claim it; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: There weren't 600 killed there. There were 60 killed, about 150 metres away from the bridge. Clirim Zhuniqi and his family from Opterusha, and then Halim Fatoshi from Bellacerkva, was shot 150 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about that. Let us try to expedite this. Was the NATO bombing going on during the event that you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: There was no NATO bombing in our area. On the 25th of March, we only saw NATO planes flying up above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw them high up there. And you also say here that at 2.00 a.m., NATO planes bombed Nogavac while you were there. Is that right? So that was another event; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: NATO did not bomb Nagavc, but it was Yugoslav planes who bombed Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so that's how it was. So the bombs were falling on Nogavac. It doesn't matter now whose bombs were there. Now, can you clarify this: You say that you still have a bullet lodged in your arm, near a wrist. Did you receive this injury during that bombing?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. No. I have one bullet in my shoulder from 25th of March, but I have eight other wounds from 2nd of April, in the village of Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that was during the bombing; right? Because on page 4, you say that you had lacerations on your head and on your right arm. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How many people were killed in that bombing? Do you know that you were severely injured, as we understood it. And can you tell us how many people were killed during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: At that time, at 1.00 in the morning, I arrived at Nagavc and I heard very well MiG planes coming from Montenegro and firing on Nagavc village. On this occasion, there were people seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All I want to know is how many people were killed in that bombing.

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know, because I was very seriously injured myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you how many people got killed in that bombing?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know. There were a lot of dead, but I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps mix up these dead with the other 60 that you claim had been killed by police?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't mix them up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a direct question: Are you trying to conceal with your statement the fact that the victims that you listed were in fact victims of NATO bombing, in view of the injuries that you described? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: NATO did not bomb the civilian population, but your planes bombed Nagavc. And German KFOR, after we returned, found bombs with Cyrillic letters on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We heard about those Cyrillic letters. Are you aware of the fact that our planes did not fly in that area at all?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I'm sure that it was the Serbian planes that bombed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what are you sure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. In that case, I'm not going to ask any questions any more. This is quite enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what case is being put about the [indiscernible] under the bridge, whether it's being suggested it was bombing or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's been suggested that it was NATO bombing, as far as I understood it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Be very brief. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understand, Mr. Zhuniqi, that the suggestion is that the people under the bridge were in some way injured, so far as the few survivors are concerned, or killed, so far as the balance are concerned, by a bomb. Any truth in that at all? That's the accused's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: They weren't wounded by bombs but by the Serbian police, whom I saw with my own eyes, with automatic rifles, and shooting all these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Nenad Matic, the man you spoke of, the man you saw after your return from Albania, when did you last see him? Where was that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: On the last occasion I saw him at the -- for the first time, I saw him at the Belaje bridge, and according to the photographs brought by KFOR, and recognised him as Nenad Matic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Seven hundred people you've described as being in the riverbed generally. That is not the number of people who were under the bridge, and you never suggested as much. Seven hundred people. How much of the village did that represent? Or, to put it another way, how many people lived in the village altogether, for this 700 to be in the riverbed?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: The village has about 350 houses, with about 3.000 inhabitants. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zhuniqi, you said that you saw the picture of Mr. Nenad Matic, and the KFOR people showed his picture; is it right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: I recognised Nenad Matic because I used to work with a bus, but I didn't know his name, and it was only when German KFOR showed me the photographs that I recognised him and identified him by name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When they showed you a picture, that picture, did it say anything about him, such as what he is doing, whether he's police or whether he's military, or something else?

utterances.speaker: ISUF ZHUNIQI
utterances.text: No. They only asked if I knew this person, and I said I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zhuniqi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until tomorrow morning, 9.00. One other change in the calendar, I'm afraid. Monday we shall be sitting from 9.00 until 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. Hendrie tomorrow. I think we've applied for 92 bis. We haven't a ruling yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've given a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm informed we have given one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll pick it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of June 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
